implementation_notes: JavaScript collapses the composite into one expression: Array.map is the splitter, the async function passed to it is the router, Promise.all is the barrier and its fulfillment array carries results in input order regardless of completion order (MDN documents exactly that), and reduce is the merge algorithm. The classic correlation state has no in-process counterpart here - the array index replaces it - and only reappears when parts travel over a real channel, where the broker's correlation facility takes over.
code_sketch:
const parts = split(order);                        // [{ kind, payload, ... }]
const results = await Promise.all(parts.map(route));   // fan-out + barrier
return results.reduce(mergeResult, emptyReport());     // aggregation
pitfalls: Promise.all rejects on the first rejection and does not cancel the remaining parts: use Promise.allSettled when a partial aggregate is acceptable, otherwise abort the losers with an AbortController.
The fan-out is unbounded: mapping a large message into thousands of simultaneous requests exhausts sockets and rate limits - chunk or pool the parts.
Mapping to async callbacks without awaiting the array (parts.map(async ...) without Promise.all) returns pending promises that are silently ignored.
